theme: The Tabernacle design begins, ark, table, lampstand
readingInstruction: Read Exodus 25:1-26:37. These chapters are a set of building instructions, so read them slowly and let your imagination build the structure as you go. Notice that the first piece of furniture described is the ark, not the courtyard or the outer tent. God starts from the center and works outward.
settingTheScene: Moses is on Mount Sinai with God, and the covenant has just been sealed (Exodus 24). Now God gives him a pattern for a tent that Israel is to build, so that the God who met them on the mountain can live in their midst. The tabernacle is a portable sanctuary, and it will travel with Israel through the wilderness. The instructions run from Exodus 25 to 31, and the building itself is told in Exodus 35 to 40. The whole project answers one question: how can a holy God live among a sinful people?
observation: The offering for the tabernacle is voluntary, from “every man whose heart moves him” (25:2).
The purpose is stated: “And let them make me a sanctuary, that I may dwell in their midst” (25:8).
Moses is told to make everything “according to the pattern” he was shown on the mountain (25:9, 40).
The ark of the covenant is a gold-covered chest with a lid called the mercy seat, and two cherubim face each other over it (25:10-22).
God says, “There I will meet with you” above the mercy seat (25:22).
The ark holds “the testimony,” the tablets of the law (25:16, 21).
The table of the bread of the Presence (25:23-30) and the lampstand shaped like a flowering almond tree (25:31-40) fill the holy place.
The tabernacle is made of curtains of blue, purple, and scarlet with cherubim woven into them, and a veil separates the Holy Place from the Most Holy Place (26:31-33).
interpretation:
The first thing to notice is the purpose. God does not ask for a building because he needs a house. He asks for it because he wants to be near his people. “That I may dwell in their midst” is the whole point. The tabernacle is a statement that the God who thundered from the mountain intends to live in a tent among them.

The second thing to notice is the order. The ark comes first, and it holds the tablets of the law. Over it is the mercy seat, the lid, and between the cherubim God says he will speak. The law is under the throne, and mercy is on top of the law. When the high priest later sprinkles blood on the mercy seat on the Day of Atonement, the picture will be complete: the demands of the law are met by a sacrifice, and the way is open for God to meet with sinners.

The third thing is the language of Eden. The tabernacle is full of garden imagery. The lampstand is a tree with branches, buds, and almond blossoms. The cherubim recall the guardians placed at the east of Eden (Genesis 3:24). The fabric of the tabernacle has pictures of cherubim on it. The entrance to the sanctuary faces east, just like Eden. The tabernacle is a small Eden, a place where God and people may meet again. What was lost in Genesis 3 is being slowly restored.

The fourth thing is the layers of holiness. Gold, blue, and purple become richer the closer you get to the center. The veil marks a boundary that only one man can cross, once a year. The building teaches that God is near, and that his nearness is dangerous to sinners unless a way is made. The next few weeks of reading will explain what that way is.

Finally, notice the phrase “according to the pattern.” Moses is not free to design the tabernacle however he likes. This is the first clue that the earthly tabernacle is a copy of something heavenly, a point the letter to the Hebrews will make.
connection: John says that the Word became flesh and “dwelt among us” (John 1:14). The Greek word means “tabernacled.” Jesus is the true dwelling place of God with man. Hebrews 8:5 says that the priests serve “a copy and shadow of the heavenly things,” quoting the instruction to make everything according to the pattern. Revelation 21:3 promises, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man.”
application:
Think about the first purpose of the tabernacle: God wanted to be near his people. Spend a few minutes thanking God that he wants to be with you, and not just to rule you.

Notice that the offering was voluntary and from the heart. Ask yourself whether your giving to God, of time and money, comes from a willing heart.

Remember that in Christ your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19). Ask God to help you live as someone in whom he dwells.
prayerPrompts: Thank God that he chose to live among his people.
Ask him to make you a willing giver.
Thank him that in Christ he has come even closer.
